title: The ground people built
teaches: How Seattle sluiced away hills and filled its tideflats, and why loose, wet fill shook hardest and liquefied in the 2001 Nisqually earthquake

blocks.text: At 10:54 on the morning of 28 February 2001, a magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck 52 kilometres beneath Anderson Island, near Olympia. It was deep, inside the subducting plate (lesson 11), so the shaking was spread out and moderate, and nobody was killed by falling debris or collapsing structures. Yet the damage in Seattle was strangely uneven. Brick buildings in Pioneer Square lost **parapets**, the low walls along their rooflines, and pieces of their outer walls. In SoDo, on Harbor Island and at Boeing Field, the ground cracked, sank and spat out fountains of sand and water, breaking a runway at Boeing Field. Up on the hills, a few kilometres away, little happened. Those hills are glacial sand, gravel and till, packed hard under a kilometre of ice.

The damage followed a map, though not a map of the fault or of distance from the epicentre. It followed a map of what the ground was made of, and people had put much of that failing ground there since the 1890s.

blocks.caption: A sand boil near El Centro, California, after the 1979 Imperial Valley earthquake: sand and water forced up through the ground, as they were in SoDo in 2001.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The deep 2001 Nisqually quake (M6.8) damaged Pioneer Square, SoDo, Harbor Island and Boeing Field.
The damage followed the ground: the worst was on young, artificial land.

blocks.text: Early Seattle was cramped between steep hills and the water, so its leaders decided to move the hills. From 1898 to 1930, in a series of **regrades**, crews sluiced Denny Hill, north of downtown, into Elliott Bay with high-pressure water cannons, and later dug it away with steam shovels and conveyors.[^spite-mounds] Other hills were cut down too. South of downtown, the wide **tideflats** at the mouth of the Duwamish River flooded twice a day. Workers filled them with dredged sand and silt and with earth from the regrades to make flat land for railways, factories and the port. Harbor Island, built between 1903 and 1909 from river and tideflat dredgings, was for a while the largest artificial island in the world.

blocks.text: The fill was dumped wet, into water, and never packed down. Its grains of sand lie loosely against each other with water in every gap. Under it, at depths of tens of metres, lies the dense glacial ground that the ice sheet packed down under a kilometre of its own weight (the first lesson of this branch). Pioneer Square, too, sits partly on fill: after a fire destroyed the old town in 1889, the streets were raised a storey on fill, leaving the old ground floors underground.[^underground]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: From 1898 to 1930 Seattle sluiced away Denny Hill and other hills, and filled the Duwamish tideflats.
Harbor Island was built from dredged river sediment, about 1903–1909.
The fill is loose, wet sand and silt; the glacial ground beneath it is dense.

blocks.text: Shake a jar of loose wet sand and it settles as the grains slip into the gaps and pack tighter. In the ground, those gaps are full of water, so when the grains try to pack down, they squeeze it. During quick shaking, the water cannot escape in time, and its pressure rises. Soon it carries part of the weight that the grains carried before, so the grains press on each other less. Once the water pressure rises enough to carry all the weight, the grains lose contact and the sand loses all its strength, flowing like a thick liquid. This is **liquefaction**.

blocks.caption: Two boxes of ground under the same shaking: dense glacial soil and loose wet fill. The numbers are illustrative.
blocks.task: Shake the fill until it liquefies

blocks.text: Buildings on liquefied ground sink and tilt, buried pipes and tanks float up, and the pressurised water escapes through cracks, carrying sand to the surface as **sand boils**. In Niigata, Japan, in 1964, whole apartment blocks tipped over intact.[^niigata] Dense glacial soil, already packed as tightly as shaking could pack it, does not liquefy. That explains the difference between SoDo and Capitol Hill in 2001, and it will matter even more in a shallow quake on the Seattle fault (two lessons back) or a great Cascadia earthquake (lesson 20).

Engineers can prevent this. They pack the fill with vibrating probes, drive stone columns through it to compact the sand and let water drain, or stand buildings on **piles**, long columns of steel or concrete driven down through the fill to the dense ground below. Much of the new waterfront was built this way, while the highway tunnel that replaced the earthquake-damaged Alaskan Way Viaduct in 2019 was bored deep through the glacial soil beneath.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Shaking packs loose wet grains; the trapped water’s pressure rises until it carries the weight.
Then the sand flows: buildings sink and tilt, and sand boils erupt.
Dense glacial soil does not liquefy; engineers pack fill or reach down to dense ground.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Seattle’s fill
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why was damage in 2001 worst in SoDo and on Harbor Island?
choices: They are built on loose, wet fill that shakes hard and can liquefy
They were closest to the epicentre
items.why: The epicentre was far away and deep; the difference was the ground.

items.ask: Where did much of the fill come from?
choices: Dredged river sediment and earth from regraded hills like Denny Hill
items.why: The city sluiced away its hills and dredged the river to fill the tideflats.

choices: Water pressure between loose grains rises during shaking until it carries the weight
items.why: Shaking packs the grains, squeezing the trapped water; its pressure takes over the load and the grains lose contact.

items.ask: Why does dense glacial soil not liquefy?
choices: Its grains are already packed tightly, so shaking cannot pack them more
items.why: With no room to pack tighter, the grains do not squeeze the water, and its pressure does not rise.

items.ask: Which is a way to protect a building on fill?
choices: Stand it on piles that reach the dense ground below
Add more loose sand on top
Water the ground before a quake
items.why: Piles carry the load past the fill; packing the fill or draining it also works.

summary: **Shaking damage follows the ground.** In the 2001 Nisqually earthquake, filled tideflats such as SoDo and Harbor Island cracked and sank while little happened on the nearby glacial hills.
**Fill dumped into water is loose and wet.** Seattle's sluiced hills and dredged sediment went into the tideflats and were never packed, leaving water in every gap between grains.
**Shaking can liquefy loose wet sand.** The grains try to pack tighter, the trapped water takes their weight, and the sand flows, so buildings sink and tilt and sand boils erupt.
**Engineers pack fill or reach dense ground.** Vibrating probes, stone columns or piles driven to the glacial soil beneath prevent liquefaction, because dense glacial ground does not liquefy.

underground.title: The Seattle Underground
underground.text: After the Great Seattle Fire of 1889, the city rebuilt in brick and raised the streets of Pioneer Square, in places by a storey or more, to lift them above the tides and give the sewers a slope. For years the pavements stayed at the old level, with ladders down from the new streets; later they were roofed over. Parts of the old street level can still be toured.

spite-mounds.title: Spite mounds
spite-mounds.text: The city could wash away its streets, but private plots required the owner's consent. Holdouts who refused to sell or pay their share of the regrade were left perched atop narrow, sheer-sided pinnacles of dirt up to 15 metres high, known as spite mounds, with houses teetering on top until the owners gave in.

niigata.title: Niigata, 1964
niigata.text: At the Kawagishi-cho apartment complex in Niigata, built on reclaimed river sand, four-storey concrete buildings stayed in one piece as the ground liquefied beneath them. One tilted by 80 degrees, nearly flat on its side, so that residents walked out onto the side of the building through their windows.
